tweets.text:
AI agent adoption is still very bimodal right now. You have coding and coding adjacent tasks which have taken off, and then everything else. 

And even within coding, you have a very wide continuum of adoption patterns, with some likely a small percentage of developers deploying background agents working on projects in parallel, and the rest of everyone else still working with agents 1:1. 

Then, there’s the entire rest of knowledge work where real agentic adoption is still very early. The reason for this is that most of the workflows still need to reengineered to work with agents. 

This isn’t the same as deploying a chat system for better research efficiency, but instead requires workflows to be rebuilt, data to be wired up in new ways, new practices for accountability and liability of decisions when agents are in the mix, governance and compliance paradigm changes, security upgrades, and more. 

We’re still so unbelievably early in what this is going to look like outside of a few categories of work right now. This is why you can basically expect 100X more agent adoption from what we’ve seen so far.

convergence to the mean

when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own.

we copy what works. borrow the language, the aesthetic, the features. we call it learning from the market, following best practices, staying competitive. together, everything starts to feel familiar. polished, interchangeable. nothing wrong. nothing alive.

the mean isn’t necessarily bad. it’s where everything lands when we remove the reasons for it to be different.

numbers are easier to compare than feelings, so we make things that produce numbers. we study what gets attention, then shape ourselves around it. eventually the feedback stops informing the work and starts authoring it. we’re no longer asking what we want to say. we’re asking what will be rewarded for saying.

ai makes this loop frictionless. it can draw from more references than we could see in a lifetime. but access to every perspective isn’t the same as having one. it hasn’t lived a particular life that makes one detail unbearable and another beautiful. when we ask it to choose for us without bringing any intention of our own, we get something plausible, easy to approve.

then we ship it, measure it, copy it, and feed it back into the next round. a tidal wave of mid.

this changes not just the work, but the people making it.

we describe ourselves in categories platforms can distribute and markets understand. designer. founder. creator. pick a niche. build a brand. be consistent. the parts that don’t fit become inconvenient, even when those contradictions might produce our most interesting work. we become easier to classify and harder to tell apart.

i think we need to approach making things more like artists.

an artist develops a perspective through the work. making, noticing, choosing, failing, returning. learning what matters even when nobody else cares. craft gives that perspective a form precise enough for someone else to experience.

the life outside the work matters too. the places you’ve lived, the people you’ve loved, the things you’re embarrassed to care about. these aren’t distractions from having something to say. they’re how you come to have something to say.

we understand this with music, paintings, photographs, movies. we expect a person to be present in the choices. we want to experience something we wouldn’t have encountered without them.

software can do this too.

a piece of software expresses beliefs about how life should feel. what deserves your attention. what you should be free to change. whether a task should feel like paperwork or play. even a small interaction can carry someone’s care, humor, or curiosity.

but we rarely talk about software as a medium. we talk about it as an industry. markets to capture, workflows to optimize, competitors to catch up with. we add a feature because someone else has it, without asking whether it belongs. products accumulate the same parts and lose what made them worth choosing.

underneath the branding, it’s all the same thing.

artists learn from others too. the question is whether you’re absorbing those influences into a point of view, or using them to avoid developing one.

what are you trying to let someone feel, understand, or do? why this particular shape? what have you noticed that the existing tools don’t seem to notice?

those questions don’t have answers you can borrow from a competitor’s roadmap.

if we can make almost anything, deciding what deserves to exist becomes more important, not less. speed gives us more chances to exercise judgment. it doesn’t remove the responsibility.

i don’t want a world where every person becomes a more efficient distributor of the same ideas. i want people to use these tools to go further into what they actually care about. to make things specific enough that we can feel someone behind them.

what is the point of everyone being able to make something, if we all end up making the same thing?

tweets.text:
AI agent adoption is still very bimodal right now. You have coding and coding adjacent tasks which have taken off, and then everything else. 

And even within coding, you have a very wide continuum of adoption patterns, with some likely a small percentage of developers deploying background agents working on projects in parallel, and the rest of everyone else still working with agents 1:1. 

Then, there’s the entire rest of knowledge work where real agentic adoption is still very early. The reason for this is that most of the workflows still need to reengineered to work with agents. 

This isn’t the same as deploying a chat system for better research efficiency, but instead requires workflows to be rebuilt, data to be wired up in new ways, new practices for accountability and liability of decisions when agents are in the mix, governance and compliance paradigm changes, security upgrades, and more. 

We’re still so unbelievably early in what this is going to look like outside of a few categories of work right now. This is why you can basically expect 100X more agent adoption from what we’ve seen so far.

convergence to the mean

when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own.

we copy what works. borrow the language, the aesthetic, the features. we call it learning from the market, following best practices, staying competitive. together, everything starts to feel familiar. polished, interchangeable. nothing wrong. nothing alive.

the mean isn’t necessarily bad. it’s where everything lands when we remove the reasons for it to be different.

numbers are easier to compare than feelings, so we make things that produce numbers. we study what gets attention, then shape ourselves around it. eventually the feedback stops informing the work and starts authoring it. we’re no longer asking what we want to say. we’re asking what will be rewarded for saying.

ai makes this loop frictionless. it can draw from more references than we could see in a lifetime. but access to every perspective isn’t the same as having one. it hasn’t lived a particular life that makes one detail unbearable and another beautiful. when we ask it to choose for us without bringing any intention of our own, we get something plausible, easy to approve.

then we ship it, measure it, copy it, and feed it back into the next round. a tidal wave of mid.

this changes not just the work, but the people making it.

we describe ourselves in categories platforms can distribute and markets understand. designer. founder. creator. pick a niche. build a brand. be consistent. the parts that don’t fit become inconvenient, even when those contradictions might produce our most interesting work. we become easier to classify and harder to tell apart.

i think we need to approach making things more like artists.

an artist develops a perspective through the work. making, noticing, choosing, failing, returning. learning what matters even when nobody else cares. craft gives that perspective a form precise enough for someone else to experience.

the life outside the work matters too. the places you’ve lived, the people you’ve loved, the things you’re embarrassed to care about. these aren’t distractions from having something to say. they’re how you come to have something to say.

we understand this with music, paintings, photographs, movies. we expect a person to be present in the choices. we want to experience something we wouldn’t have encountered without them.

software can do this too.

a piece of software expresses beliefs about how life should feel. what deserves your attention. what you should be free to change. whether a task should feel like paperwork or play. even a small interaction can carry someone’s care, humor, or curiosity.

but we rarely talk about software as a medium. we talk about it as an industry. markets to capture, workflows to optimize, competitors to catch up with. we add a feature because someone else has it, without asking whether it belongs. products accumulate the same parts and lose what made them worth choosing.

underneath the branding, it’s all the same thing.

artists learn from others too. the question is whether you’re absorbing those influences into a point of view, or using them to avoid developing one.

what are you trying to let someone feel, understand, or do? why this particular shape? what have you noticed that the existing tools don’t seem to notice?

those questions don’t have answers you can borrow from a competitor’s roadmap.

if we can make almost anything, deciding what deserves to exist becomes more important, not less. speed gives us more chances to exercise judgment. it doesn’t remove the responsibility.

i don’t want a world where every person becomes a more efficient distributor of the same ideas. i want people to use these tools to go further into what they actually care about. to make things specific enough that we can feel someone behind them.

what is the point of everyone being able to make something, if we all end up making the same thing?

tweets.text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.
tweets.summary_zh:
我们将花更多时间理解语言模型的输出。这里有一些小建议：

- 可以让语言模型使用一种叫 ASD-STE100 的清晰语言来解释内容，这样写出来的东西更易读。
- 试着让它画图，图比文字更容易理解。
- 直接要求生成网页（用 HTML），效果会很漂亮，还能加动画啥的。
- 最酷的想法是让它创建定制的解释视频，讲解任何主题，只需稍微调整一下输入就好。

总的来说，随着语言模型越来越强大，它们可以自动完成很多工作，我们的工作将更多集中在理解和监督上。而且，语言模型还可以帮助我们创造以前认为不可能的定制软件，挑战一下，你可能会收获惊喜！

tweets.text:
There's a huge opportunity right now in being the deployment layer for AI into the economy. The amount of work it takes to change out workflows in enterprises tends to be far greater than anyone realizes or would prefer. Clearly this is what the applied layer of AI is going to look like in the form of software and agents, but also it opens up new services firms opportunities.

Legacy systems need to be moved to the cloud, data organization and access needs to be updated, software needs to be connected to agents in new ways, workflows need to be reengineered for agents, HITL needs to be figured out for the process, evals need to be generated and maintained, and the entire system needs to be continually updated as new models get released and new capabilities emerge. And the full list may even be longer.

AI is not the same as just deploying software. Software you generally did the implementation of an existing, well understood category of technology, then stepped back and the customer kept running. With AI agents, you're delivering actual work augmentation to the organization, which has a completely different set of complexities associated with it. You're no longer deploying tools that the company is merely enabled by, you're deploying work output in a process. Completely different implementation and enablement process.

As a result, this is going to open up lots of new kinds of firms and plays for existing firms to diffuse AI into organizations. We're going to see approaches by industry, by size of company, and by problem inside of companies. Traditional SIs will modernize and adapt (some will clearly not adapt as well), and new entrants will also be founded in this period that take advantage of this window. Great time to be an FDE or FDE firm.

I asked Secretary Duffy what Americans should be able to do, if we get this decade right, that they can't do today.

Sean Duffy is the Secretary of Transportation, and he sat down with me at our Startup Industrial Base event in DC today. He went straight to how our country's air traffic gets managed.

At the command center, people sit in front of six screens with a paper flight chart above them, trying to make the calls on weather and routing.

His example: four planes reach the same runway at the same time and only one can land. See it two hours out, speed up two, slow one down, and each one lands when the runway is open. "Like, not complicated stuff, but we don't do any of this."

Paper and pencil and minimal human augmentation from software looks like this: Say an airport can take 15 planes in a 15 minute window. "Well, the airlines will schedule 32." He says he's handing the airlines that data and asking them to spread out.

The tool is SMART, from Air Space Intelligence, a small company he says competed with the biggest companies and won. It predicts. His stage example: a 2.5 hour ground stop might only need 45 minutes. He's taken heat for supposedly handing air traffic control to AI. Duffy's answer? "it's dumb AI, not smart AI." Controllers still make every call.

None of this needs a breakthrough. It needs the will of the people to know they need to use software and be ok with AI augmentation instead of insisting on a paper chart and copper wire.

tweets.text:
Two random honest thoughts on the market right now..

First is on people: It's harder than ever to find missionaries. I'm seeing people leave the companies they have cofounded to join the "obvious" winners. Public CEOs are leaving for positions at labs. Founders leaving and rejoining neolabs at a moment's notice. Companies getting Windsurf-ed where only the choice people are getting to join the future company. Founders raising tranched valuations without worrying about the next employee that will join them will have 409As that make early exercising impossible. 

As early stage VCs, we are often just betting on people. And, when those people leave on a dime's notice, then the remaining company (usually) becomes a shell. It seems like a great time to be a mercenary, and everyone feels like one even though there are missionaries out there. 

Second is on defensibility: There's a lot of chatter on moats, so I won't re-litigate the matter here. But the thing that I want to call out is given the pace of what's happening the moat is no longer "one" thing. Like if you really think about it especially in the app layer - the harness is like a thousand small things done well. And, a lot of it is invisible. And given the competition is so fierce and new entrants overnight, you really have to dig into the details to figure out why a given company is different. What is their edge, and their combined edge across product, tech and GTM. 

And often times even with that, you end up going back to "well the real defensibility is the founders". And in those founders the defensibility is their speed of execution and being able to adapt to the market. That has become the new bar for every founder out there, given there are no "blue ocean" markets. And even if there are, any company with a LITTLE bit of heat, will have a lot of competitiors overnight. 

Even though I think I have a pretty good sense on finding the best people who have founder market fit, I find this current climate really hard and it's testing all my priors (and patience) at the same time. 

I know it's not true, but feels like everyone is in it to grab the bag and not really care about their legacy of what they want to build (please reach out if you do).

tweets.text:
At Box, we've been testing Sonnet 5.5 in early access on our complex work eval with the Box Agent, and Sonnet 5.5 is another strong jump from Sonnet 5 on knowledge work with enterprise content.

Across the board we saw a 4 pt overall improvement on our hardest tests, but it was roughly 2.4× faster to a finished deliverable on 12% fewer tokens. We also saw major wins in key verticals, like a +18 percentage point improvement in Financial Services, +7 pt in Legal, +8 pt in Life Sciences, and +7 pt in the Public Sector. 

Here are some specific wins on certain tasks that show the power of Sonnet 5.5:

* Financial services (+48 points): a due-diligence review of a trading-tool acquisition, where the deal book's arithmetic doesn't hold up. Sonnet 5.5 caught the miscalculated interest totals and the mispriced options and flagged them, and it also finished this work about 61% faster.

* Legal (+14 points): a commercial lease review. Sonnet 5.5 refused to invent a "standard" market benchmark for renewal terms and notice periods, and instead flagged what the lease was genuinely missing.

* Life sciences (+22 points): writing up a field trial from the raw measurement data. Sonnet 5.5 got the sample standard deviations right across both treatment groups. Sonnet 5 missed nearly all of them. And Sonnet 5.5 did it about 41% faster.

* Public sector (+11 points): a report on a math intervention program. Sonnet 5.5 pulled the right student progress-monitoring figures out of the underlying data, about 71% faster.

Customers will be able to build AI agents with Sonnet 5.5 in the Box AI Studio shortly.

tweets.text:
Interesting to think about all the implications in a world where agents begin to make the best or most efficient choice for their users.

On one hand, there is some subset of the economy that benefits from the friction customers traditionally have changing something about their habits. In those parts of the market, switching costs will come down and competition is going to increase dramatically until some equilibrium is reached between the disruptive alternatives and the incumbents.

On the other hand, there are lots of markets that are hurt by a significant amount of friction, where agents will begin to unlock all kinds of economic activity by making it far easier to buy products or services that were too frictionful before. Healthcare, travel, local services, certain information services, and other entirely new markets probably are net beneficiaries of agents as a result.

No matter what, a future meaningfully mediated by agents that work tirelessly for us and our goals can’t possibly function exactly the same as today. Going to be wild.

本视频为每年的开发者大会（DevDay 2026）的现场直播，涵盖了最新的AI技术发展、产品创新及其在各行各业的应用。与会者分享了如何运用AI工具提升创意设计流程以及未来的行业趋势。

podcasts.name: Greg Isenberg
podcasts.title: OpenAI DevDay: Dots, Agents & $100B Opportunities
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频讨论了OpenAI在开发日（DevDay）上发布的新工具和技术，包括用于创意和自动化的“代理”（Agents），以及如何利用这些新机遇在未来1000亿美元的市场中获得成功。它详细介绍了OpenAI的最新动态，以及这些技术如何影响企业和个人的创造力和工作效率。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 视频中提到的AI工具和自动化解决方案，能够为Logic Labs和TexTale在创意设计和电商领域带来重要启示。

podcasts.name: Stanford GSB
podcasts.title: Ep79 How to Make Your University’s Board of Trustees More Useful
podcasts.summary_zh:

💡 值得一看 — 视频中的董事会治理理念和管理策略对于发展 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 的品牌运营思考有启发，特别是关于如何利用外部资源来增强业务影响力的讨论。

podcasts.name: The AI Daily Brief
podcasts.title: How to Build Team Agents
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频讨论了如何构建团队代理（Team Agents），利用 AI 技术提升团队协作和效率。它介绍了一些实用的方法和工具，帮助团队成员更好地沟通与合作，从而实现更高的生产力和创新。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 这个话题直接相关于 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 的团队管理和合作，能够为你的 AI 应用和创意设计过程提供灵感。

podcasts.name: TBPN
podcasts.title: 🔴 LIVE from OpenAI DevDay
podcasts.summary_zh:
该视频是关于 OpenAI DevDay 大会的直播，讨论了 OpenAI 最新的产品发布和技术进展，包括对 AI 工具的增强功能，以及如何影响开发者和企业的应用场景。内容涵盖了行业前沿的趋势和开发者所面临的挑战，适合对 AI 和创意设计有兴趣的观众。

podcasts.title: The Real Risks of AI Agents
podcasts.summary_zh:
视频探讨了 AI 代理的潜在风险，包括它们在决策过程中的不透明性和可能对人类决策造成的影响。视频还分析了如何在开发和部署 AI 代理时，确保安全性和道德性，以减少这些风险的发生。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 这对 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 的产品开发有直接影响，同时也能帮助你理解如何在创意设计中更安全地利用 AI 技术。

这个视频邀请了 TypeSafe 的 CEO，他谈论了自己对公开基准测试在 AI 领域应用的看法。他认为公开基准测试可能会导致误导，并分享了一些关于如何更有效评估 AI 模型的观点。

💡 值得一看 — 该视频涉及一些科技和行业动态，可能对Yves在Logic Labs和TexTale的创意设计中提供一些启发，尤其是在如何利用AI强化个人助手的应用方面。

podcasts.name: Y Combinator
podcasts.title: Robotic factories that build robots
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频讲述了一个独特的概念：用机器人工厂来建造机器人。这种新兴技术展示了如何通过自动化提升生产效率，可能会在未来改变制造业的面貌。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 这个内容与 AI 工具在创意设计以及可能影响电商运营的趋势息息相关，适合 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 的发展思路。

podcasts.name: Fireship
podcasts.title: DHH has gone completely off the rails...
podcasts.summary_zh:
这段视频主要讨论了开发者领军人物 DHH（David Heinemeier Hansson）近期的一些极端言论和观点，特别是在商业模式和软件开发方向上的独特看法，引发了广泛的讨论和争议。视频深入分析了这些言论背后的逻辑，以及对整个技术行业可能产生的影响。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — DHH 的观点可能会对 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 在创意设计和电商运营中的思考产生启发，帮助了解行业内的不同声音和趋势。

podcasts.name: Greg Isenberg
podcasts.title: $5T opportunity: AI Roll Ups
podcasts.summary_zh:
视频探讨了人工智能的整合机会，特别是如何通过收购和合并不同的 AI 初创公司来实现巨大的市场潜力。Greg Isenberg 强调了这类整合能够带来的价值，并分析了当前市场的一些成功案例。

podcasts.name: Peter Yang
podcasts.title: Sonnet 5.5 is Here! It's Insane at Making Videos (7 Incredible Examples)
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频介绍了Sonnet 5.5这个新发布的工具，展示了其在视频制作方面的强大功能，提供了七个令人惊叹的示例，说明它如何能够快速而轻松地生成高质量视频内容。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — Sonnet 5.5作为一个可以极大提高创意设计效率的AI工具，可能会对Logic Labs和TexTale的项目产生直接的积极影响。

producthunt.name: Ami AI
producthunt.summary_zh: Ami AI 是一款智能客户互动工具，旨在帮助企业与客户建立更有效的沟通。它利用人工智能技术，自动回复客户咨询、提供产品信息，提升客户满意度。通过个性化服务，Ami AI 让企业更轻松地管理客户关系。

producthunt.name: tiun.
producthunt.tagline: Auth, billing, and payments for AI builders
producthunt.summary_zh: tiun.是一款专为人工智能开发者设计的工具，提供身份验证、计费和支付功能。它简化了开发过程中与用户账户和支付相关的管理，使AI项目更容易上线和运营。

producthunt.name: CREEM 2.0
producthunt.tagline: Sell and grow your AI built products
producthunt.summary_zh: CREEM 2.0是一款用于销售和推广人工智能产品的平台。它为用户提供了工具和资源，使他们能够轻松创建、销售和扩展基于AI的产品，帮助用户实现商业增长。

producthunt.name: Jev
producthunt.tagline: Fast, structured AI decisions for software automation
producthunt.summary_zh: Jev是一款智能软件自动化工具，能够快速、精准地根据结构化数据做出决策。它简化了复杂的业务流程，提高了工作效率。用户可以轻松通过Jev实现自动化操作，节省时间和资源。

producthunt.name: Clueso MCP
producthunt.tagline: Create and edit videos by chatting
producthunt.summary_zh: Clueso MCP 是一款通过聊天方式创建和编辑视频的工具。用户可以通过文字对话来生成视频内容，这使得视频制作变得简单快速。它支持实时编辑，让创作过程更加灵活。

producthunt.name: Mastra Factory
producthunt.tagline: From issue to production, run by agents.
producthunt.summary_zh: Mastra Factory 是一个自动化平台，专为管理生产流程而设计。用户可以通过平台提交问题，从而直接将其转化为生产任务，整个过程由代理人进行协调与执行。简而言之，它简化了产品从问题到生产的转化流程。

producthunt.name: Voiskey
producthunt.tagline: AI voice typing that sounds right in every app
producthunt.summary_zh: Voiskey是一款人工智能语音输入工具，可以在各类应用中实现准确的语音转文字功能。用户只需说话，Voiskey即可实时将语音转换为文字，让写作更加便捷。无论是聊天、文档还是社交媒体，都能轻松使用。

producthunt.name: Naoma AI Demo Agent V2
producthunt.tagline: Turns website traffic into booked, qualified meetings
producthunt.summary_zh: Naoma AI Demo Agent V2是一款智能工具，能够将网站访问者转化为预约的合格会议。它利用人工智能分析访客行为，提高转化率，简化预约流程。通过这款产品，企业可以更有效地管理潜在客户互动。

producthunt.name: Switch
producthunt.tagline: Bring any AI agent into Slack, Teams & Discord
producthunt.summary_zh: Switch是一款可以将各种AI助手集成到Slack、Teams和Discord中的工具。用户可以通过这个平台轻松接入不同的AI代理，以提高团队的沟通和协作效率。它简化了工作流程，让员工能够快速获取所需的信息和支持。

producthunt.name: AINA
producthunt.tagline: Find your job search blind spots with an AI coach
producthunt.summary_zh: AINA 是一款人工智能教练，旨在帮助求职者发现他们在求职过程中可能忽视的盲点。通过个性化分析和建议，AINA能够提升求职者的竞争力和面试准备。这个工具确保你能全面了解自己的求职策略，提升成功率。

producthunt.name: Anysite.io
producthunt.tagline: Build and enrich B2B lists by chatting to your agent
producthunt.summary_zh: Anysite.io 是一个可以让用户通过聊天与智能助手互动的平台，用于创建和丰富B2B（企业对企业）的潜在客户名单。用户只需与助手对话，就能快速获取和整理所需的商业信息。这个工具简化了数据收集过程，提高了工作效率。

producthunt.name: Superset Mobile
producthunt.tagline: Your coding agents, now in your pocket
producthunt.summary_zh: Superset Mobile 是一款移动应用，专为编码者设计。用户可以在手机上轻松访问代码助手，获取编程建议和解决方案，随时随地提高编码效率。

producthunt.name: ProductBridge
producthunt.tagline: AI-native customer support and feedback agent
producthunt.summary_zh: ProductBridge是一款基于人工智能的客户支持和反馈助手。它能够自动回答用户问题，并收集用户反馈，帮助企业更高效地管理客户关系。产品使企业能够提供即时服务，提高客户满意度。

producthunt.name: Kilo Code for iOS and Android
producthunt.tagline: Start coding agents, control sessions, review PRs. Anywhere.
producthunt.summary_zh: Kilo Code是一款移动应用，支持iOS和Android系统。用户可以随时随地编写代码、管理会话和查看代码提交记录（PR）。该产品旨在提高开发者的灵活性和工作效率。

producthunt.name: Monospace from Directus
producthunt.tagline: The governed API layer for every app, person, and agent
producthunt.summary_zh: Monospace from Directus 是一个管理型 API 层，旨在为各种应用、用户和智能代理提供统一的数据访问方式。它简化了数据管理流程，让用户可以轻松获取和操作所需的信息。通过直观的界面，用户能够高效地构建和管理自己的数据应用。

github_trending.description: The design language that makes your AI harness better at design.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目旨在提供一种设计语言，帮助用户更好地利用人工智能进行创作和设计。对于Yves来说，这个项目对Logic Labs（AI公司）有帮助，因为它可以促进AI在设计领域的应用，为产品创新提供灵感；同时，对TexTale（科技服装电商）方面也有价值，能够提升品牌的视觉效果和用户体验，吸引更多消费者。作为创意设计从业者，Yves可以利用这个工具激发更具创意的设计想法。

github_trending.description: Marketing skills for Claude Code and AI agents. CRO, copywriting, SEO, analytics, and growth engineering.

github_trending.description: Give your AI agent eyes to see the entire internet. Read & search Twitter, Reddit, YouTube, GitHub, Bilibili, XiaoHongShu — one CLI, zero API fees.

对 Yves 来说，这个项目可以帮助 Logic Labs 在AI领域获取更广泛的数据源，从而提高 AI 模型的训练和应用效果，同时也能为 TexTale 提供更精准的市场洞察和趋势分析，助力品牌营销。

github_trending.description: Developer-first error tracking and performance monitoring
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目 Sentry 是一个帮助开发者追踪错误和监测应用性能的工具，能够让他们及时发现和修复问题，确保软件运行顺利。对于 Yves 来说，Sentry 可以帮助 Logic Labs 提高 AI 应用的质量和用户体验，同时也能够为 TexTale 提供更稳定的电商平台，确保顾客在购物时不遇到技术问题。此外，作为创意设计从业者，使用 Sentry 能让他更专注于设计，而不必担心技术上的漏洞。

github_trending.description: World's first open-source, agentic video production system. 12 production pipelines, 100+ tools, 700+ agent skill and production-knowledge files. Turn your AI coding assistant into a full video production studio.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个开源的视频制作系统，提供超过100种工具和12条制作流程，可以帮助用户利用AI进行视频创作。对于Yves来说，这一项目可以极大提升他在Logic Labs中的创意输出，帮助AI更好地实现视频营销和宣传内容的制作。此外，对TexTale的产品展示和品牌宣传也会带来显著的视觉效果和创意提升。
这个项目是一个基于 TypeScript 的全栈开发框架，旨在简化和加快 Web 应用程序的开发过程，让开发者更高效地构建应用。对Yves来说，它可以为Logic Labs提供快速迭代和原型设计的基础，帮助他在AI项目中实现更具创意的想法；同时，也可以支持TexTale在电商平台上开发更灵活的功能，提升用户体验。

github_trending.description: Fast and extensible multi-platform HTTP/1-2-3 web server with automatic HTTPS
github_trending.summary_zh: Caddy 是一个快速且灵活的多平台网络服务器，可以自动处理 HTTPS 加密，让网站更加安全和易于访问。对于 Yves 来说，Caddy 可以在 TexTale 的电商平台上提供更好的网站性能和安全性，提高用户体验，同时也能为 Logic Labs 提供可靠的服务器支持，助力 AI 应用的部署。作为创意设计从业者，Caddy 也有助于简化网站的搭建和管理流程，让他专注于创意设计和品牌营销。
